title: Performance Model for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Workflows
authors: Pooja Rao, Dimitar Trenev, Jerome Gonthier, Taylor Patti, Sebastian Stern, Tyler Takeshita, Yuri Alexeev, Cedric Lin, Sam McArdle, Justin Lietz, Katherine Klymko, Ermal Rrapaj, Norm Tubman, Krysta Svore, Peter Komar, Elica Kyoseva
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical workflows are expected to underpin practical quantum computing applications, yet the quantum and HPC communities lack a shared framework for reasoning about where and when their integration requirements matter most. Such a framework must separate two distinct levels of analysis: the application level, where communication overhead affects runtime performance, and the real-time level, where it determines feasibility. To address this, we introduce a runtime model that decomposes workflow execution into quantum compute, classical compute, and communication costs. At the application level, a communication-to-computation ratio from this decomposition quantifies whether a workflow is communication-bound or compute-bound; at the real-time level, a feasibility constraint determines whether timing requirements can be met at all, with the reaction time setting the logical clock speed of fault-tolerant computation once they are. Application of this model to representative workflows demonstrates that co-location of quantum processors with HPC infrastructure offers negligible performance benefit for compute-intensive applications today, while tight integration remains crucial for real-time tasks such as quantum error correction needed for large scale quantum computations. However, we discuss how even at the application level these assessments may shift with hardware evolution, illustrating how the model can identify specific crossover conditions, and how, under fault tolerance, the reaction time can set application-level performance.
summary: This paper introduces a comprehensive runtime model to analyze hybrid quantum-classical workflows, separating performance concerns into abstract application levels and strict real-time physical constraints. It demonstrates that while communication overhead can be quantified by a ratio, achieving fault tolerance requires careful consideration of timing feasibility dictated by the underlying hardware coherence times.
main_problem: The field lacks a shared framework for analyzing performance when integrating quantum processors with classical High-Performance Computing (HPC) resources in hybrid workflows.
main_result: A runtime model decomposes workflow execution into quantum, classical, and communication costs, allowing quantification of whether the bottleneck is computation or communication at different operational regimes.
method: The authors introduce a comprehensive runtime model that analyzes performance at both an abstract application level (using communication-to-computation ratios) and a physical real-time level (using feasibility constraints).
model_or_system: The system analyzed is the hybrid quantum-classical workflow, decomposed into $	ext{T}_{	ext{cycle}} = 	ext{T}_{	ext{C}} + 	ext{T}_{	ext{Q}} + 	ext{T}_{	ext{comm}}$. The analysis distinguishes between application-level timing (logical qubits) and real-time constraints (physical coherence times).
key_observables: Communication-to-computation ratio ($	ext{R}_{	ext{cc}}$), Real-time feasibility constraint, Logical error probability ($P_L(r)$)
important_parameters: Classical/Quantum Costs ($	ext{CC}, 	ext{CQ}$), Communication Latency ($L$), Bandwidth ($B$), Physical coherence time ($	au_{	ext{phys}}$), Code distance ($d$)
main_assumptions: The model assumes distinct levels of analysis (application vs. real-time) and provides specific formulas for decomposing cycle time components.

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for a shared framework, then introduces the runtime model decomposing costs into three components. It analyzes performance across application and real-time regimes, applies this to various algorithms (like SQSP-MaF), and finally discusses error accumulation in fault tolerance.
why_interesting: It provides essential architectural guidelines by quantifying when hardware co-location benefits are negligible versus when tight integration is mandatory for feasibility, which guides the roadmap for quantum hardware development.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 The compute cycle: a complete round trip of information between the classical host and quantum accelerator. The total cycle time Tcycle = TC + TQ + Tcomm decomposes into classical compute time (TC), quantum compute time (TQ), and communication overhead (Tcomm). At the real-time level, classical processing and communication must satisfy TC,step + Tcomm,step ≤τ phys to preserve correctness.

Fig. 2 Compute cycle for Sample-Based Quantum Diag- onalization (SQD). The standard workflow (solid lines) performs a single quantum sampling phase followed by classical subspace construction and diagonalization. The closed-loop variant (dashed lines) iteratively refines the cir- cuit ansatz based on diagonalization results. In both cases, the communication frequency is F = 1 per iteration, yield- ing a low communication-to-computation ratio (Rcc ≪1).

Fig. 3 Compute cycle for the Generative Quantum Eigen- solver (GQE), assuming training from scratch. The trans- former samples operator index sequences that define quan- tum circuits, whose measured energies provide the training signal. The classical cost is dominated by the backprop- agation step (logit-matching loss), while the transformer forward pass (sampling) is computationally trivial. As with SQD, the workflow is quantum-dominated due to the large shot budget required for energy estimation.
